 By Audrey Noble October 28, 2026 Smile Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story If scalp care is hair care, then we know to turn to K-beauty for the ultimate hair-washing routine. But its approach goes beyond innovative ingredients and cleansing techniques to deliver strong, sleek strands. As Beth Stokes, associate director of marketing at Dr. Groot, explains, the Korean way of washing hair is a more holistic, preventative philosophy than Western hair-washing routines, which focus solely on cleansing. “It prioritizes the scalp as the foundation for healthy, resilient hair, treating it much like skin,” Stokes says.
 Y. Claire Chang](https://www.unionderm.com/doctors/dr-claire-chang/){: target="_blank"}, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Union Derm, adds: “Korean beauty has helped make scalp care feel like an important part of self-care and a daily routine, rather than something you only think about when you develop problems like dandruff, itching, or hair thinning. Instead of focusing only on making the hair look shinier or smoother, the approach considers both scalp health and hair health as connected.”
 To wash your hair the Korean way, consider the following:
 The Staple Ingredients
 You can expect to see many skin-care ingredients alongside traditional Korean hair ingredients in shampoos, scalp scrubs, conditioners, and masks. These include salicylic acid, niacinamide, Centella, and panthenol, as well as black bean, black sesame, kelp, and rice water, says Sarah Chung Park , founder and CEO of Landing International. With newer formulations, she says PDRN and exosomes are moving into scalp ampoules to better support healthy hair growth. The goals, she says, are the same as for your face: clean, calm, and balanced.
 “Your scalp is skin,” Park says. “It gets oily, dry, irritated, and it ages, just like your face. Korean consumers already know so much about skin care that taking care of the scalp feels like the natural next step.”
 Hair Vinegar
 Vinegar rinses have been around for years in Korean hair care as a traditional home remedy but aren’t really a staple today. Though vinegar’s acetic acid is known to smooth the hair’s surface and add shine, Stokes says the effect is temporary, and there’s little scientific evidence that it improves scalp health or helps with hair regrowth .
 “What’s popular now is hair vinegar,” Park says. “[It’s] a product made just for the scalp. You apply it after shampooing, massage it in, and rinse. Koreans love it for oily scalps, buildup, and scalp odor, which gets worse in hot, humid summers.”
 The Process
 Each hair-wash routine will differ based on your personal needs, but generally speaking a Korean hair-wash routine includes the following steps:
 A Scalp Pretreatment Dr. Chang says this is an occasional step and not something you need for every wash. Some people use a scalp scaler or exfoliating treatment before shampooing to remove excess sebum, dead skin cells, and product buildup.

 Targeted Shampoo Dr. Chang says to choose shampoo based on scalp concerns (excess oil, sensitivity, flaking, etc.) rather than just dry or damaged hair. So pick formulations with soothing ingredients to support scalp health. Park says that you’ll wash your hair with lukewarm water and massage it in for about a minute. “A lot of Koreans use a silicone scalp brush for this,” she adds. “It cleans more deeply and feels like a mini head massage.”
 Korean shampoos are having a moment in the States. She points to products like the Lador Tea Tree Calming Scalp Shampoo , which uses tea-tree oil and menthol to control excess sebum and flakes while also providing a cooling sensation, or the Lilyeve Grow:Turn Shampoo , which supports scalp health over time.
 Conditioning Hair Treatment “These focus on improving softness, smoothness, and manageability while reducing friction and breakage,” Dr. Chang says. You’ll typically apply them to the midlengths and ends of your hair, unless they’re specifically formulated for the scalp. You can also use occasional intensive treatments, such as hair masks, protein treatments, scalp packs, or vinegar-based rinses.
 Celebrity hairstylist Mark Townsend , who says he didn’t see true innovation in the scalp-care space until using K-beauty products, loves the Dr. Groot Miracle In Shower Scalp & Hydrating Treatment . Use it after shampooing; it contains salicylic acid, rosemary oil, and biotin to hydrate hair, exfoliate the scalp, and promote healthy hair growth. “Star of the show,” he says. “The results have been incredible. My clients that have switched over to the Dr. Groot shampoos and treatment have seen a major improvement in the health of their hair, which makes styling so much easier for me.”
 You’ll end your hair routine with a leave-in scalp tonic or serum, which she says adds targeted support to address specific scalp concerns. Then, without adding excessive heat or friction, dry the scalp thoroughly. If these steps and products feel overwhelming to start, no worries. Park says you can focus on three steps to wash your hair the Korean way: “A good scalp shampoo, a treatment, and drying your scalp completely,” she says.
